strengths: MU-Mis addresses a practically useful setting: unlearning using only the pretrained model and forgetting data, without retained-data access or stored training trajectories. The input-gradient objective is an interesting heuristic.

Full-class results are promising. On CIFAR-100, MU-Mis achieves zero forgetting accuracy while retaining 76.32% accuracy, compared with 76.36% before unlearning. The face-recognition results also compare favorably with the evaluated alternatives.
The evaluation includes full-class, subclass, and random-subset tasks, retraining references, several baselines, and runtime comparisons.

Table 6 provides useful evidence that both objective terms matter: their combination achieves 76.32% retained accuracy versus 60.45% for target-class suppression alone, with zero forgetting accuracy in both cases.
weaknesses: The central theoretical derivation in Section 3.2 contains substantive errors. Differentiation with respect to training inputs omits derivatives of the loss gradient and the dependence of subsequent parameters on those inputs. The claimed symmetry equating g_k g_k'^T with g_k' g_k^T also fails generally for vector-valued outputs. Moreover, small individual cross-sample terms do not establish that their sum is negligible. Consequently, the claimed approximation of training contribution by input sensitivity is not established.

The objective lacks a convincing connection to removing training influence. Local input sensitivity is different from counterfactual sample deletion. In particular, adding a shared input-dependent function h(x) to every logit preserves all softmax probabilities while changing the squared-gradient difference in Equation 1. This exposes a degeneracy in interpreting loss reduction as forgetting; sensitivity plots and attention maps do not resolve it.

The random-subset experiment is largely non-diagnostic. In Table 5, both the unchanged pretrained model and MU-Mis obtain 94.67% retained accuracy and 100% forgetting accuracy; their MIA scores differ by only one percentage point. With only 100 samples removed, the reported metrics do not establish meaningful improvement over doing nothing.

Privacy evaluation is insufficiently informative. MIA reports only the fraction of forgetting samples classified as members, without false-positive rates, calibration, or uncertainty. The retrained model itself receives a 94% membership score in Table 5, highlighting the need to distinguish attack miscalibration from residual information. Stronger calibrated attacks and comparisons with retrained-model output distributions are needed to support the privacy claims.

The experimental scope and comparisons do not support claims of consistent, significant superiority. All experiments use ResNet18, with few selected classes and one random deletion size. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, making small gains such as 0.26 percentage points over SSD difficult to assess. SalUn is cited but not evaluated, baseline tuning is insufficiently documented, and larger deletion fractions or sequential requests are unexplored.

Essential implementation details are missing or inconsistent. The stopping threshold delta is never specified, including how it is selected without retained data. Algorithm 1 initializes the accumulated loss to zero but never updates it, so its stopping statistic does not track optimization; the outer repeat also undermines the stated iteration limit. The transition from summed, unsquared sensitivity norms to squared norms with one randomly sampled alternative class needs justification. These issues prevent faithful reproduction and leave stability unresolved.
